extracted.intended_audience: literate readers, poets, and critics (Spectator readership / general literary public)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for evaluating and producing the diction of an heroic/epic poem (esp. Miltonian/Blank Verse): what qualities the language must have and the methods to attain them, with cautions about excess. Also includes related prescriptive remarks on social behaviour, delicacy, and constitutional liberty found in the same essays.

rubrics_metrics.name: Language of an Heroic Poem: perspicuous and sublime
rubrics_metrics.description: It is requisite that the Language of an Heroic Poem should be both Perspicuous and Sublime.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Both qualities are necessary: perspicuity is primary (a reader forgives small slips if the sense is clear), but sublimity elevates the poem above prose and common speech. Failure in either produces an imperfect language for epic poetry.

rubrics_metrics.name: Primacy of perspicuity
rubrics_metrics.description: Perspicuity is the first and most necessary Qualification; a good-natur'd Reader sometimes overlooks a little Slip even in the Grammar or Syntax, where it is impossible for him to mistake the Poets Sense.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Minor grammatical or syntactical blemishes may be pardoned when the thought is great and natural (examples cited from Milton). Still, clarity of sense takes precedence over formal correctness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid idiomatic/common speech
rubrics_metrics.description: A Poet should take particular Care to guard himself against Idiomatick Ways of Speaking; the most obvious Phrases ... become too familiar to the Ear, and contract a kind of Meanness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not rely on ordinary conversational phrases which may sound mean in poetry; seek elevated expressions that avoid becoming vulgar through common use (cites Ovid and Lucan as examples of failing here).

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid false sublime / affectation of greatness
rubrics_metrics.description: He must not swell into a false Sublime, by endeavouring to avoid the other Extream. ... The Affectation of Greatness often hurts the Perspicuity of the Stile.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be cautious of affected grandiloquence (examples: Æschylus at times, Claudian, Statius, Shakespear and Lee). Pursue genuine elevation, not mere padding or stiffness that obscures meaning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of metaphors to raise language
rubrics_metrics.description: First, by the Use of Metaphors: Such are those of Milton.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Employ bold but just metaphors; they should not be so frequent or conflicting that they create an enigma or riddle. Milton's metaphors are cited as well-chosen—avoid thick-sowing metaphors that clash with one another.

rubrics_metrics.name: Employ idioms/structures from other tongues (Hellenisms, Latinisms, Hebraisms)
rubrics_metrics.description: Another way of raising the Language, and giving it a Poetical Turn, is to make use of the Idioms of other Tongues. ... Milton has infused a great many Latinisms, as well as Græcisms, and sometimes Hebraisms, into the Language of his Poem.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use foreign idioms, transposition of words, post-positive adjectives, turning adjectives into substantives, etc., to lift diction out of prose; but do so naturally and judiciously.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lengthening phrases and manipulating syllables
rubrics_metrics.description: The third Method ... is the lengthning of a Phrase by the Addition of Words ... as also by the extending or contracting of particular Words by the Insertion or Omission of certain Syllables.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Vary phrase-length and meter by inserting/omitting words and adjusting syllables (elisions, suppressed syllables) to give variety to numbers. Milton's use of these techniques is noted as judicious within the limits of English.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of archaic/solemn vocabulary and coinages
rubrics_metrics.description: The same Reason recommended to him several old Words, which also makes his Poem appear the more venerable, and gives it a greater Air of Antiquity. I must likewise take notice, that there are in Milton several Words of his own coining...
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Introduce venerable or old-fashioned words and, where fitting, neologisms to lend weight and antiquity; compare to Homer/Homeric liberties. Use sparingly to avoid obscurity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Moderation / judicious intermixture of unusual words
rubrics_metrics.description: A judicious intermixture is requisite ... In the employment of all the species of unusual words, moderation is necessary: for metaphors, foreign words, or any of the others improperly used, and with a design to be ridiculous, would produce the same effect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not compose diction entirely of metaphors or foreign words—such excess produces an enigma or barbarous jargon. Balance unusual elements with clarity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Blank verse demands pomp of sound and energy
rubrics_metrics.description: This Redundancy ... was the more proper for his use, because his Poem is written in Blank Verse. Rhyme, without any other Assistance, throws the Language off from Prose, and very often makes an indifferent Phrase pass unregarded; but where the Verse is not built upon Rhymes, there Pomp of Sound, and Energy of Expression, are indispensably necessary to support the Stile.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When writing in blank verse, compensate for lack of rhyme by using elevated diction, sound, and expressive energy to prevent prose-like flatness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Vary meter/numbers to avoid monotony
rubrics_metrics.description: He has with great Judgment suppressed a Syllable in several Words, and shortned those of two Syllables into one, by which Method ... he has given a greater Variety to his Numbers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use elisions and metric innovation judiciously to vary rhythm so the verse does not cloy the ear; maintain musical variety in long narrative poems.

rubrics_metrics.name: Perspicuity vs ornament: pardonable inadvertencies
rubrics_metrics.description: Such little Blemishes as these, when the Thought is great and natural, we should ... impute to a pardonable Inadvertency, or to the Weakness of human Nature, which cannot attend to each minute Particular, and give the last Finishing to every Circumstance in so long a Work.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Critics should exercise candour and not cavil at small faults when outweighed by the poem's larger merits; writers should prioritize thought even if minute finish is sometimes imperfect.

rubrics_metrics.name: An unaffected behaviour is a charm; avoid false carelessness
rubrics_metrics.description: An unaffected Behaviour is without question a very great Charm; but under the Notion of being unconstrained and disengaged, People take upon them to be unconcerned in any Duty of Life.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not mistake being unconcerned for virtue; affectation of carelessness (professing to be the 'carelessest Creature') is vanity and often masks laziness or neglect of duty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid affectation of perpetual hurry or feigned busyness
rubrics_metrics.description: Opposite to this Folly is another no less unreasonable, and that is the Impertinence of being always in a Hurry. ... These Persons who are just a going somewhere else should never be detained; all the World allow that Business is to be minded.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Feigning constant haste to appear important is an inexcusable vanity when one has no real business; it betrays superficiality and inattention to present obligations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Standard of delicacy: truth and virtue, not squeamishness
rubrics_metrics.description: True Delicacy, as I take it, consists in Exactness of Judgment and Dignity of Sentiment ... A false Delicacy is Affectation, not Politeness. What then can be the Standard of Delicacy but Truth and Virtue?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Delicacy should align with moral truth and virtue; do not soften or euphemize vice by giving 'fair Names to foul Actions'—that confuses moral judgment and diminishes natural horror of evil.

rubrics_metrics.name: Expose vice for public good (moral censure over polite euphemism)
rubrics_metrics.description: It is hoped therefore, Sir, that you will not lay aside your generous Design of exposing that monstrous Wickedness of the Town ... The Unchaste are provoked to see their Vice exposed, and the Chaste cannot rake into such Filth without Danger of Defilement; but a meer SPECTATOR may look into the Bottom, and come off without partaking in the Guilt.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Public exposure of vice serves the public good and moral education; a detached commentator can reveal corrupt practices without becoming complicit, but must do so with the aim of reformation rather than prurience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preservation of liberty via mixed legislature
rubrics_metrics.description: Liberty is best preserved, where the Legislative Power is lodged in several Persons, especially if those Persons are of different Ranks and Interests; ... The greatest Security a People can have for their Liberty, is when the Legislative Power is in the Hands of Persons so happily distinguished that ... they are providing for the whole Body of the People.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A mixed government with multiple branches representing varied ranks/interests secures liberty; one legislative body risks tyranny, two bodies lack a casting voice, and three provides balance (regal, noble, popular).
